title: Money in Code: Minor Units, Rounding and Currency
objectives: Carry amounts as integer minor units with a currency code, in storage and in JSON
Round once, at a stated step, with a stated rule, and allocate remainders so splits add up
Convert currencies with a recorded rate, and make money endpoints reject a reused key with a changed amount

cards.title: Amounts on the wire and in the database
cards.body: A binary double cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and many JSON parsers, including JavaScript’s, read every number as a double. Store money as an integer count of the currency’s minor unit (₹499.99 is 49,999 paise) or as a fixed-scale decimal, and send it the same way: {"amount": 49999, "currency": "INR"}, or a decimal string such as "499.99". The ISO 4217 code says how many minor digits to use: INR and USD have 2, JPY has 0, and KWD has 3.

cards.title: Worked example: splitting ₹100 three ways
cards.body: ₹100 is 10,000 paise, and 10,000 ÷ 3 is 3,333 with 1 paisa left over. Rounding each share to ₹33.33 charges ₹99.99 in total, so one paisa vanishes from the books. Instead give everyone the floor (3,333) and hand the leftover units out one at a time by a fixed rule, such as to the payer first: 3,334 + 3,333 + 3,333 = 10,000. The shares differ by at most one paisa and always add up.

cards.title: From request to stored amount
cards.body: The amount is made exact at the edge and rounded only where a rule says so.
steps: The request carries {"amount": "499.99", "currency": "INR"}
Look up INR’s minor digits in ISO 4217: 2
Parse the string exactly into 49,999 paise; reject a third decimal place
Apply tax or discounts in integers and exact decimals, rounding once with the named mode
Store 49,999 with INR; format as ₹499.99 only when displaying

cards.title: Rounding and conversion: choose the rule and the moment
cards.body: Two decisions change totals. The mode: half-up turns 2.5 into 3, while half-even (banker’s rounding) turns 2.5 into 2 and 3.5 into 4, which removes the upward bias over millions of roundings. The moment: three items at ₹10.10 with 18% tax give 3 × ₹1.82 = ₹5.46 if tax is rounded per line, but ₹5.45 if it is computed once on ₹30.30. Currency conversion follows the same rule: multiply the source minor units by the rate in exact decimal, round once into the target’s minor units, and store the rate and source amount alongside the result.

cards.title: Trap: a retry that changes the amount
cards.body: Idempotency keys stop a retried payment from charging twice, but only if the server checks that the retry is the same request. If a client bug reuses the key for a ₹5,000 payout after a ₹500 one, replaying the stored ₹500 result hides the bug, and running the new request breaks the key’s promise. Store a hash of the request body with the key, replay only when it matches, and reject a mismatch with an error. The IETF Idempotency-Key draft suggests 422 Unprocessable Content for this case, and Stripe’s API, for example, also returns an error when a key is reused with different parameters.

questions.prompt: Which JSON body is safest for a payment amount sent to an API?

choices.label: {"amount": 49999, "currency": "INR"}
{"amount": 499.99, "currency": "INR"}

questions.explanation: a: a JSON number like 499.99 is read as a double by many parsers, and the currency is missing. b: correct, an integer count of paise is exact in every parser up to 2^53, and the code says what the unit is. c: a formatted display string depends on locale (“1,234.50” or “1.234,50”) and has to be parsed by guesswork. d: the currency helps, but the amount is still a float on the way in.

questions.prompt: An API stores amounts for INR and JPY accounts as integer minor units. What must travel with each amount?

choices.label: The exchange rate on the day it was created
Its ISO 4217 currency code
A flag saying whether it was rounded
How many decimals the app displays

questions.explanation: a: a rate is needed only when converting, not to know what the stored number means. b: correct, the code tells you the unit, and INR has 2 minor digits while JPY has 0, so 500 means ₹5.00 or ¥500. c: a rounding flag does not say what the unit is. d: display settings vary by screen; the currency code is the stable fact.

questions.prompt: ₹100 is split between 3 people in paise. Which result keeps the books balanced?

choices.label: 3,333 paise each, writing off the extra paisa
3,333.33 paise each, kept as decimals
3,334 paise each, the payer covering 2 more

questions.explanation: a: the books are short by one paisa on every split. b: correct, floors plus one leftover unit handed out by a fixed rule sum to exactly 10,000. c: a paisa cannot be charged in thirds, so this only postpones the rounding. d: charging 10,002 paise collects more than the bill.

questions.prompt: Half-even (banker’s) rounding is applied to ₹2.5 and ₹3.5, rounding to whole rupees. What are the results?

choices.label: 3 and 4
2 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 3

questions.explanation: a: that is half-up, which always rounds .5 upwards. b: correct, half-even rounds .5 to the nearest even digit, so the ups and downs cancel out over many values. c: that is half-down or truncation. d: that is half-odd, a rarely used mode.

questions.prompt: A client retries POST /payouts with the same Idempotency-Key, but the amount has changed from ₹500 to ₹5,000. What should the server do?

choices.label: Pay ₹5,000, since the latest request wins
Replay the stored ₹500 result as a success
Reject it: the key belongs to another request
Pay the ₹4,500 difference as a top-up

questions.explanation: a: running a new request under an old key breaks the promise that one key means one operation. b: the client believes ₹5,000 went out when only ₹500 did, and the bug stays hidden. c: correct, a key names one request; comparing a stored hash of the body exposes the client bug at once. d: inventing a top-up guesses at intent and moves money nobody asked for.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for charging an INR card for a $12.99 price.

items.label: Multiply exactly: 1,299 × 83.2715 = 108,169.6785 paise
Parse "12.99" USD into 1,299 cents
Store 108,170 INR with the rate and the 1,299 USD source amount
Fetch the USD-to-INR rate and record it with its time
Round once, half-even, to 108,170 paise

questions.explanation: Parse into exact units first, use one recorded rate, keep full precision through the multiplication and round only at the end, then store enough to repeat and explain the conversion later.

questions.prompt: An app splits ₹100 bills three ways, rounds each share to ₹33.33 and drops the leftover paisa. It does 200,000 such splits a day. How many rupees go unaccounted for each day?
assumptions: One paisa is lost per split
questions.explanation: Sanity check: that is about ₹7.3 lakh a year of drift from one rounding rule, which reconciliation will flag even though each single split looks fine.

flashcards.front: How should money travel and be stored?
flashcards.back: As integer minor units (or a decimal string or fixed-scale decimal) plus an ISO 4217 currency code.
2 and 4: .5 goes to the even neighbour, so bias cancels out.
Reject it: a key names one request, so a changed body is a client bug, not a retry.

sources.title: RFC 8259: JSON, section 6 on numbers and interoperability
IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field
Martin Fowler: Money (Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture)

mechanism.title: How money stays exact from request to storage
steps: Parse money at the edge into an exact type. A request carrying “499.99” or 49999 with “INR” becomes 49,999 minor units with the code INR, using the number of minor digits that ISO 4217 lists for the currency; a value with more decimals than the currency allows is rejected, not rounded silently. From then on, adding and subtracting are integer operations, which are exact.

Multiplication and division are where rounding enters: tax, discounts, interest, conversion and splits. Each produces a fraction of a minor unit that has to be rounded. Do it once, at a step you name (per line or per invoice), with a mode you name (half-up, half-even), and keep the unrounded rate or price in the record so the calculation can be repeated and explained later.

Splits need allocation, not rounding. Dividing 10,000 paise three ways gives three floors of 3,333 and a remainder of 1. Hand the remainder out one unit at a time by a deterministic rule, such as largest fractional part first or a fixed party order. The same rule, applied on refund, reverses each share exactly, so a partially refunded group bill does not leave a stray paisa behind.

Conversion uses one recorded rate. Fetch the rate once for the operation, keep it as an exact decimal with enough digits (often 6 or more), multiply the source minor units by it, and round once into the target’s minor units. Store the source amount and currency, the rate, its source and time, and the result, so a refund can reverse the same conversion rather than using today’s rate by accident.

Endpoints that move money are idempotent and strict about it. The idempotency key is stored with a hash of the request body and the result, in the same transaction as the money write. A matching retry gets the stored result; a mismatched body under the same key is rejected. The bookkeeping itself, balanced ledger rows and reconciliation, is an architecture topic of its own; this lesson stops at the API and the stored amount.

useWhen: Any system that charges, refunds, splits, converts or reports money.
Public payment and payout APIs, where clients in many languages parse your amounts.
avoidWhen: Avoid floats for money anywhere, including JSON payloads and analytics totals that finance will compare.
Avoid converting with a fresh rate on refund; reuse the rate stored with the original charge.

rows: Needs the currency to know the unit
Scale must cover rates and tax
Totals drift by fractions of a paisa

numbers.title: Per-line or per-invoice tax rounding
steps: Per line: ₹10.10 × 0.18 = ₹1.818, which rounds to ₹1.82.
Three lines: 3 × ₹1.82 = ₹5.46 of tax.
Per invoice: ₹30.30 × 0.18 = ₹5.454, which rounds to ₹5.45.
The two rules differ by 1 paisa on this invoice; across many invoices the gap adds up and must match what the tax return reports.
numbers.result: Neither rule is wrong; mixing them is. Pick the one the rules or contract require and use it in invoices, credit notes and reports alike.

india.title: Paise, GST lines and a dollar price
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: an Indian marketplace shows ₹499.99 on screen but its API sends 49999 with INR and stores the same. Tax on each invoice is computed either per line or on the invoice total, and the business picks one rule and applies it to invoices, credit notes and refunds so the totals reconcile with its tax filings. For a seller who prices in dollars, checkout converts once with a stored rate and keeps both amounts, so a refund a month later returns exactly what was charged. Retried payment calls carry an idempotency key, and a key reused with a different amount is rejected and logged as a client bug.

pitfalls.trap: “A double is precise enough for rupees.”
pitfalls.say: “Doubles cannot hold 0.1 exactly; I’d carry paise as integers with the currency code, in JSON too.”

pitfalls.trap: “Round each share and the totals will work out.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d allocate the remainder by a fixed rule so the shares always sum to the bill.”

takeaways: Carry money as integer minor units with an ISO 4217 code, on the wire and at rest.
Round once, at a named step, with a named mode.
Convert with one recorded rate and keep it with the result.
Reject an idempotency key reused with a different body.

interactive.title: Splitting ₹100 three ways
interactive.prompt: A bill-split feature computes 100 ÷ 3 in floating point, rounds each share to two decimals and charges three cards. What does finance see when it adds up the charges for this bill?

choices.label: ₹99.99 charged against a ₹100 bill
choices.feedback: Right: each share rounds down to ₹33.33, and the leftover paisa belongs to nobody.

choices.label: Exactly ₹100, since the rounding cancels out
choices.feedback: All three shares round the same way, so nothing cancels; the error is one paisa every time.

choices.label: ₹100.02, since each share rounds up
choices.feedback: 33.333… is below the halfway point, so half-up rounding takes it down, not up.

interactive.reveal: Work in paise and allocate: 10,000 ÷ 3 gives three floors of 3,333 and a remainder of 1, which goes to one person by a fixed rule. The shares become 3,334, 3,333 and 3,333 and always add up to the bill.

seeAlso.why: Idempotency keys are what stop a retried payment from posting twice
How numbers are encoded in JSON and other formats decides whether amounts survive the trip
Double-entry ledgers record every money movement as balanced entries, in the minor units this lesson stores

title: Dates, Time Zones and Daylight Saving in Business Logic
objectives: Store past instants in UTC and keep the IANA zone for anything tied to a person’s or a place’s calendar
Schedule future local events from a local time plus zone, not a precomputed UTC instant
Handle daylight-saving gaps and overlaps, and compute “today” in the zone that defines it

cards.title: Instants, local times and zones
cards.body: An instant is one point on the timeline, such as when a payment was captured; store it in UTC, for example in PostgreSQL’s timestamptz, which normalises to UTC. A local date and time like “09:00 on 3 March” is not an instant until you add a zone. A zone is an IANA identifier such as Asia/Kolkata or America/New_York, not an offset like +05:30: offsets change with daylight saving and with law, while the identifier carries the rules. India uses +05:30 all year; New York switches between −05:00 and −04:00.

cards.title: Worked example: a 9 a.m. reminder across a clock change
cards.body: A user in New York sets a daily 09:00 reminder in January, and the service stores it as 14:00 UTC. That works until 8 March 2026, when New York moves to UTC−4: 14:00 UTC is now 10:00 local, an hour late, every day until November. Store the rule instead, 09:00 with zone America/New_York, and compute each run’s UTC instant from it: 14:00 UTC in winter, 13:00 UTC in summer.

cards.title: Scheduling the next run of a local-time job
cards.body: The stored rule stays in local time; only the next run becomes a UTC instant.
steps: Stored: 09:00 every day, zone America/New_York
Take the next local date: 9 March 2026
Ask the time-zone database for that date’s offset: UTC−4 after the 8 March change
09:00 local becomes 13:00 UTC; enqueue the job for that instant
After it runs, repeat from the next local date, never by adding 24 hours

cards.title: Gaps and overlaps
cards.body: On a spring-forward day, US clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 does not exist. On the autumn day, clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 happens twice. Libraries resolve both with a policy: for a gap, usually move forward; for an overlap, pick the earlier or later offset. Choose on purpose: a nightly job at 02:30 should still run once on the gap day, and one at 01:30 should run once, not twice, on the overlap day. Those days are also 23 and 25 hours long, so “add one day” and “add 24 hours” give different answers.

cards.title: Trap: “today” in the server’s zone
cards.body: A daily spending limit resets at midnight. If the code takes the date from the server clock in UTC, an Indian user’s day starts at 05:30 IST, so a purchase at 03:00 IST on 5 March counts towards 4 March. Compute business dates in the zone that defines them, whether the user’s, the merchant’s or the one a contract names, and store that zone with the record. Run servers in UTC and never let a result depend on the host’s zone setting.

questions.prompt: A payment was captured. What should the database store for when it happened?

choices.label: The local time in the user’s zone, no zone kept
The UTC instant, in a zone-aware timestamp type
The server’s local time, without any zone
Only the calendar date, as YYYY-MM-DD

questions.explanation: a: without the zone, nobody can tell later which instant it was, or order it against other events. b: correct, a past event is a fixed instant, and UTC in a zone-aware type compares and sorts correctly everywhere. c: the server’s zone can change with a migration, and the value carries no record of it. d: a date alone loses the order of events and the time needed for disputes.

questions.prompt: A user in New York picks their time zone in settings. What should the service save?

choices.label: −05:00, the offset on the day they signed up
EST, the abbreviation shown in the app
America/New_York, the IANA zone name
The hours between their zone and the server’s

questions.explanation: a: New York is −04:00 for most of the year, so a fixed offset is wrong for months at a time. b: abbreviations are ambiguous (CST is used for US Central, China and Cuba) and carry no daylight-saving rules. c: correct, the identifier carries the rules, past and future, through the time-zone database. d: it ties the user’s data to wherever the server happens to run.

questions.prompt: A 09:00 weekly meeting for a London team was saved in January as 09:00 UTC. What happens after UK clocks go forward on 29 March 2026?

choices.label: It starts at 10:00 local, an hour late
It starts at 08:00 local, an hour early
It stays at 09:00, as UTC adjusts itself
It is skipped on the day of the change

questions.explanation: a: correct, in summer London is UTC+1, so 09:00 UTC is 10:00 local. b: that would need London to move behind UTC, which it never does. c: UTC never changes; that is why a fixed UTC instant drifts against local time. d: an instant set in UTC always exists; only local times can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A job runs at 02:30 New York time every night. What happens on 8 March 2026, when clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00?

choices.label: The time does not exist; a policy must move it
It runs twice, once at each 02:30
It runs at 02:30 UTC that night instead
Nothing: every local time exists every day

questions.explanation: a: correct, 02:00 to 02:59 is skipped that night, so the library or your code must choose, usually 03:00. b: repeated times happen on the autumn change, not the spring one. c: nothing converts a local schedule to UTC on its own. d: on spring-forward days an hour of local time is missing.

questions.prompt: An app on UTC servers resets each user’s daily limit at server midnight. When does the limit reset for users in India?

choices.label: At 00:00 IST
At 05:30 IST
At 18:30 IST
At 23:30 IST

questions.explanation: a: that would need the reset computed in Asia/Kolkata, not in UTC. b: correct, India is UTC+05:30, so midnight UTC is 05:30 IST. c: that subtracts the offset instead of adding it; 18:30 IST is 13:00 UTC. d: no offset between UTC and IST gives this.

questions.prompt: Order how a service computes the next run of “09:00 daily, America/New_York”.

items.label: Convert 09:00 on that date to a UTC instant
Pick the next local calendar date
Enqueue the job at that instant
Read the stored local time and zone
Look up that date’s UTC offset in the time-zone database

questions.explanation: The rule stays local; the offset is looked up for the specific date, so the conversion is right on both sides of a clock change.

questions.prompt: New York’s clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00 on 1 November 2026. How many hours long is that local day, midnight to midnight?
assumptions: Local midnight to the next local midnight
One hour of local time repeats
questions.workedAnswer: 24 hours of clock time + the repeated hour from 01:00 to 02:00 = 25 hours
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the spring-forward day is 23 hours, so a job that adds 24 hours to its last run drifts an hour at each change.

flashcards.back: An instant is one point on the timeline, stored in UTC; a local time needs a zone to become one.

flashcards.front: Store an offset or a zone?
flashcards.back: The IANA zone, such as Asia/Kolkata; offsets change with daylight saving and with law.
Store 09:00 plus the zone and compute each UTC instant when it is needed.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

mechanism.title: How a service handles time from request to schedule
steps: At the API edge, timestamps arrive as RFC 3339 strings with an offset, such as 2026-03-05T09:00:00+05:30, and become instants. A string with no offset is either rejected or read in a zone the API documents, never silently in the server’s. Responses send instants in UTC or with an explicit offset.

Instants are stored in UTC in a zone-aware type, and servers run with UTC as their zone, so nothing depends on where a container happens to start. Durations, such as a token valid for 3,600 seconds or a timeout, are arithmetic on instants and need no zone.

Anything defined by a person’s or a place’s calendar is stored as a local date or time plus an IANA zone: a recurring reminder, a shop’s opening hours, a billing period that ends at local midnight, a flight’s departure. It becomes an instant only when needed, using the time-zone rules current at that moment.

Those rules change several times a year as governments move or abolish daylight saving. Keep the time-zone database in the operating system, runtime and database up to date, and recompute stored future instants after an update; this is the second reason not to precompute UTC instants for local events.

Calendar arithmetic happens in local terms: “tomorrow at 09:00” adds a calendar day and then converts. Gaps and overlaps are resolved by an explicit policy, and tests cover one spring-forward and one fall-back date in a zone that observes daylight saving, not just Asia/Kolkata, which does not.

useWhen: Reminders, schedules, opening hours, billing periods and daily limits.
Any product with users in more than one zone, or in one that observes daylight saving.
avoidWhen: Avoid storing future local events as fixed UTC instants.
Avoid relying on the server’s zone, or treating offsets such as +05:30 as zones.

rows: Date + the zone that defines it

numbers.title: How long is a day?
assumptions: New York, which observes daylight saving
1 November 2026: clocks go from 02:00 back to 01:00
steps: On an ordinary day, midnight to midnight is 24 hours.
On 8 March, one local hour is skipped, so the day is 23 hours.
On 1 November, one local hour repeats, so the day is 25 hours.
A job that adds 24 hours to its last run moves an hour on the clock at each change; one that adds a calendar day stays at 09:00.
numbers.result: Calendar days and 24-hour durations are different units. Use calendar arithmetic in the local zone for schedules, and durations for timeouts and expiries.

india.title: A daily cashback cap for users in India and the Gulf
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a payments app caps cashback at ₹500 per user per day. Its servers run in UTC, and the first version reset the cap at UTC midnight, which is 05:30 in India and 04:00 in Dubai, so late-night shoppers found part of the next day’s cap already used. The fix stored each user’s IANA zone (Asia/Kolkata, Asia/Dubai), computed the business date in that zone for every transaction, and kept the instant in UTC for audit. Neither zone observes daylight saving today, but the team still stored the zone rather than a fixed offset, so a future rule change needs only a time-zone database update.

pitfalls.trap: “We store everything in UTC, so time zones are solved.”
pitfalls.say: “UTC is right for past instants; for future local events I’d store the local time and IANA zone and convert when needed.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add 24 hours to get tomorrow’s run.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add a calendar day in the user’s zone, because days around clock changes are 23 or 25 hours.”

takeaways: Store past instants in UTC in a zone-aware type.
Store future local events as local time plus IANA zone.
Choose gap and overlap policies and test both dates.
Compute business dates in the zone that defines them, never the server’s.

interactive.title: Scheduling by adding 24 hours
interactive.prompt: A reminder service schedules each next run by adding 24 hours to the last one. A user in New York set it for 09:00 in February. When does it fire on 9 March 2026, after the clocks went forward on 8 March?

choices.label: At 10:00 local, an hour late
choices.feedback: Right: 8 March had only 23 hours, so 24 hours after 09:00 on 7 March is 10:00 on 8 March, and every run after keeps that hour.

choices.label: At 09:00 local, as the user set it
choices.feedback: That needs calendar arithmetic in the user’s zone; a fixed 24-hour step ignores the clock change.

choices.label: At 08:00 local, an hour early
choices.feedback: Spring forward removes an hour, so a fixed 24-hour step lands later on the clock, not earlier.

interactive.reveal: Store 09:00 with America/New_York and compute each run from the next calendar date in that zone. Durations suit timeouts and expiries; calendar arithmetic suits schedules.

seeAlso.why: Wall clocks and monotonic clocks: which one to read for timestamps and which for durations
Scheduled jobs that run at a local time are enqueued by a scheduler like this
Timestamps in APIs travel as RFC 3339 strings with an explicit offset
Formatting those stored instants for each user’s locale and time zone on the front end

title: Text in a Backend: Unicode, Normalisation and Length Limits
objectives: Tell bytes, code points and user-perceived characters apart, and name the unit of every limit
Normalise text before comparing it or making it unique, such as usernames and emails
Prevent corrupted text from wrong encodings, cut characters and narrow database character sets

cards.title: Bytes, code points and characters
cards.body: UTF-8 stores each Unicode code point in 1 to 4 bytes: “a” takes 1, “é” 2, “₹” and Devanagari letters such as “न” 3, and most emoji 4. What a reader sees as one character can be several code points: “नि” is “न” plus the vowel sign “ि”, and a family emoji joins several emoji with invisible joiners. So “length” has at least three answers: bytes for storage and wire limits, code points for many databases’ VARCHAR(n), and grapheme clusters for what the user counts.

cards.title: Worked example: one name, two encodings
cards.body: “José” can be stored with “é” as one code point (U+00E9, the NFC form) or as “e” followed by a combining acute accent (U+0065 U+0301, the NFD form). They look identical but compare unequal, so a uniqueness check lets “José” register twice and a search for one misses the other. The NFC form is 4 code points and 5 bytes; the NFD form is 5 code points and 6 bytes. Normalise to one form, usually NFC, at the edge, before storing, comparing or hashing.

cards.title: Text from request to storage
cards.body: Bytes become text once, are normalised once, and every later step works on the same form.
steps: Decode the request body as UTF-8; reject invalid byte sequences
Normalise the text to NFC
For identifiers, also build a case-folded key and check it against lookalike rules
Check each limit in the unit the rule names, such as 30 visible characters
Store in a UTF-8 column; compare and index the normalised key

cards.title: Identifiers: usernames and emails
cards.body: For uniqueness, “Asha”, “asha” and “ASHA” are usually meant to be one account. Keep what the user typed for display, plus a canonical key (normalised, then case-folded) with the unique index on the key. Case-folding is not the same as lowercasing: under full case folding the German “ß” becomes “ss”. Lookalikes such as Latin “a” and Cyrillic “а” let “pаypal” pass a uniqueness check, so restrict usernames to one script or check confusables as Unicode TS #39 describes. For email, the domain is case-insensitive; RFC 5321 lets the local part be case-sensitive, but most providers ignore case, so many services compare a lowercased copy.

cards.title: Trap: cutting text by bytes
cards.body: Truncating at a byte count can split a 3-byte character, leaving invalid UTF-8: some databases reject the row, and others store a replacement character “�”. A 100-byte limit on a Hindi name allows only about 33 code points. Truncate on grapheme cluster boundaries and size byte limits for 4-byte characters. On MySQL, the legacy utf8 character set (utf8mb3) holds at most 3 bytes per character, so emoji are rejected or mangled; use utf8mb4.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does the word “भारत”, 4 code points of Devanagari, take in UTF-8?

choices.label: 4 bytes
8 bytes
12 bytes
16 bytes

questions.explanation: a: that counts code points, not bytes. b: that is the UTF-16 size, where each of these code points takes 2 bytes. c: correct, every Devanagari code point takes 3 bytes in UTF-8, so 4 × 3 = 12. d: 4 bytes per code point applies to emoji and other characters beyond U+FFFF, or to UTF-32.

questions.prompt: Two accounts named “José” exist although usernames are unique. They look identical and contain no spaces. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: Two Unicode forms of “é”: one code point or two
The unique index ignores the case of letters
The two rows were written by different servers
UTF-8 encodes the same “é” at random each time

questions.explanation: a: correct, NFC “é” is U+00E9 while NFD is “e” plus U+0301, so the strings differ although they render the same; normalising at the edge fixes it. b: ignoring case would merge more names, not allow duplicates. c: the server that wrote a row does not change what a unique index compares. d: UTF-8 is deterministic; the same code points always give the same bytes.

questions.prompt: Usernames must be unique regardless of case. What should the unique index cover?

choices.label: The username exactly as the user typed it
A normalised, case-folded key of the name
The lowercased name, without normalising
A hash of the username as the user typed it

questions.explanation: a: “Asha” and “asha” would both be accepted. b: correct, normalising then case-folding makes every spelling of the same name collide, while the typed form is kept for display. c: lowercasing misses names that differ only in Unicode form, and does not fold “ß” to “ss”. d: hashing the typed form keeps every difference the typed form had.

questions.prompt: A customer’s name “José” appears as “JosÃ©” in an email the service sent. What happened?

choices.label: UTF-8 bytes were decoded as Latin-1 somewhere
The name was normalised to NFD before sending
The database cut off the last character
The email client’s font lacks a glyph for “é”

questions.explanation: a: correct, “é” is two bytes in UTF-8 (C3 A9), and reading them as Latin-1 shows “Ã©”; this is called mojibake. b: NFD text renders the same as NFC. c: a cut would lose “é” or leave “�”, not add a character. d: a missing glyph shows as a box, not as two other letters.

questions.prompt: A MySQL table using the legacy utf8 character set rejects a review containing “🎉”. Why?

choices.label: That utf8 holds at most 3 bytes per character
Emoji are not part of the Unicode standard
The review must be normalised to NFC first
Full-text indexes accept only ASCII text

questions.explanation: a: correct, MySQL’s legacy utf8 is utf8mb3, and “🎉” needs 4 bytes; utf8mb4 stores it. b: emoji are Unicode code points like any other. c: normalisation does not change the emoji, which has no decomposition. d: full-text indexes in MySQL handle non-ASCII text; the column’s character set is the limit.

questions.prompt: Order how a sign-up endpoint handles a username.

items.label: Build the case-folded key and check lookalike rules
Insert, relying on the unique index on the key
Decode the body as UTF-8, rejecting invalid bytes
Check the length in visible characters
Normalise the name to NFC

questions.explanation: Text must be valid before it can be normalised, the key is built from the normalised form, limits are checked on the final text, and the database index is the last word on uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A display-name column allows 64 bytes. Names are written in Devanagari, which takes 3 bytes per code point in UTF-8. Roughly how many code points fit?
assumptions: No emoji or Latin letters mixed in
questions.workedAnswer: 64 bytes ÷ 3 bytes per code point ≈ 21 code points
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a reader sees fewer than 21 characters, because vowel signs join the letter before them, so state limits in visible characters and size the byte column for the worst case.

flashcards.back: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point; one visible character can be several code points.
The same text can have different code points (“é” or “e” plus an accent); NFC makes equal text compare equal.
Index a normalised, case-folded key, keep the typed form for display, and guard against lookalikes.

sources.title: RFC 3629: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
W3C: Character Model for the World Wide Web: String Matching
RFC 8265: Preparation, Enforcement and Comparison of Usernames and Passwords (PRECIS)

mechanism.title: How text stays correct through a service
steps: Bytes become text in one place. Request bodies are decoded as UTF-8, which RFC 8259 requires for JSON exchanged between systems, and invalid sequences are rejected with a 400 rather than replaced silently. Inside the service everything is text until it is encoded again at an edge: the database driver, a file, an outgoing request.

Text is normalised at the edge to NFC so that equal-looking text has equal code points. NFKC goes further and folds compatibility characters, such as the full-width “Ａ” to “A” and the “ﬁ” ligature to “fi”; that suits identifiers and search keys, not text you will show back unchanged.

Identifiers get a canonical key: normalise, case-fold, then apply identifier rules such as allowed scripts and no invisible characters outside the scripts that need them. The unique index and every lookup use the key; the typed form is kept only for display.

Every limit names its unit. Storage and wire limits are in bytes; user-facing limits are usually grapheme clusters; database column lengths depend on the engine. Validate in the unit the user sees, make sure the byte budget fits the worst case of 4 bytes per code point, and truncate only on grapheme boundaries.

UTF-8 is used end to end: database and connection character sets (utf8mb4 on MySQL), exported files with the encoding declared, and outgoing email with properly encoded headers. Sorting and case-insensitive comparison use a collation chosen on purpose, because alphabetical order differs between languages.

useWhen: Sign-up, usernames, search, names and addresses: anything people type.
Services whose users write in more than one script.
avoidWhen: Avoid comparing or hashing user text before normalising it.
Avoid truncating by bytes or code points where a person can see the cut.

rows: What a reader sees as one character

numbers.title: One name, three lengths
assumptions: Devanagari letters and vowel signs take 3 bytes each
steps: Code points: न, ि, श, ा = 4.
Grapheme clusters: “नि” and “शा” = 2, which is what a reader counts.
A 10-byte limit rejects this two-character name, while a 10-code-point limit counts it as 4 of 10.
numbers.result: Pick the unit for each limit on purpose, and size byte budgets for the worst case of 4 bytes per code point.

india.title: Handles on a social app used across India
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a social app lets people choose handles in English, Hindi and Tamil. Within weeks it found handles that looked identical but were distinct: “rahul” in Latin letters and “rаhul” with a Cyrillic “а”, and names pasted from documents in NFD form. The fix normalised every handle to NFC at the edge, stored a key made with NFKC and case folding under a unique index, allowed one script per handle plus digits, measured the 30-character limit in grapheme clusters, and sized the column for 4 bytes per code point.

pitfalls.trap: “A string’s length is just its length.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d name the unit: bytes for storage, grapheme clusters for what users see.”

pitfalls.trap: “Lowercase the username and put a unique index on it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d normalise, case-fold and check lookalikes, index that key, and keep the typed form for display.”

takeaways: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point, and a visible character can span several code points.
Normalise to NFC at the edge before comparing, hashing or storing.
Index a canonical, case-folded key for identifiers, and guard against lookalikes.
Name the unit of every limit and never cut text mid-character.

interactive.title: Truncating a Hindi name to 10 bytes
interactive.prompt: A service cuts display names to their first 10 bytes before saving them to a UTF-8 column. A user signs up as “निशा शर्मा”. What happens?

choices.label: The cut splits a character, leaving invalid UTF-8
choices.feedback: Right: three code points take 9 bytes, so the tenth byte is the first of the fourth, and the row is rejected or saved with “�”.

choices.label: The name is saved as its first 10 letters
choices.feedback: 10 bytes hold at most 3 whole Devanagari code points, not 10 letters.

choices.label: Nothing goes wrong: byte cuts never split UTF-8
choices.feedback: Most characters outside ASCII span several bytes, so a byte cut can land inside one.

interactive.reveal: Measure the limit in the unit users see, truncate on grapheme cluster boundaries, and size byte columns for 4 bytes per code point.

seeAlso.why: Decoding and normalising text is the first step in handling untrusted input
Serialisation formats fix the encoding text travels in; length and form are up to the service
Forms are where user text first arrives, with client-side length checks that should match the server
Translated and right-to-left text the backend must store and count correctly

title: Request and Response Fields: Mass Assignment and Over-Exposure
objectives: Spot mass assignment, where a request sets fields its caller should not control
Accept writes through explicit allowlists of fields per endpoint and role
Return only the fields each caller may see, through explicit response shapes

cards.title: The model is not the API
cards.body: Many frameworks can copy a JSON body straight onto a database model, as in user.update(req.body). The model has fields its caller must never set: role, email_verified, balance, tenant_id, created_by. If the handler copies everything, a request carrying "role": "admin" makes the caller an admin. This is mass assignment, also called over-posting. OWASP’s API Security Top 10 (2023) groups it with over-exposed response fields under API3, broken object property level authorisation.

cards.title: Worked example: a profile update that grants admin
cards.body: PATCH /me accepts {"name": "Asha"} and the handler sets every key in the body as a column on the caller’s row. An attacker sends {"name": "Asha", "role": "admin", "email_verified": true}. Both extra keys are real columns, so the update succeeds. The fix is an input type for this endpoint holding only name, avatar and bio; any other field is rejected with a 400, and role changes go through a separate admin endpoint with its own authorisation check and audit record.

cards.title: Explicit shapes in and out
cards.body: A request is parsed into the endpoint’s own type, and the response is built from another.
steps: The body arrives: {"name": "Asha", "role": "admin"}
Parse it into the endpoint’s input type: name, avatar and bio only
The unknown field role is rejected with 400, or dropped and logged
Check which allowed fields this caller may change, then update the model
Map the model to the response type for this caller; never serialise it whole

cards.title: Over-exposed responses
cards.body: The mirror-image bug is returning the whole row: the user object goes out with password_hash, mfa_secret and internal notes, and the app simply does not display them. Anyone can read the raw JSON. Define a response type per view: a public profile has name and avatar, the owner also sees their email, and an admin also sees the last sign-in address. Nested objects need the same care: an order list that embeds the full seller object leaks the seller’s phone number to every buyer.

cards.title: Trap: a denylist of protected fields
cards.body: “Copy everything except role and is_admin” fails the day someone adds a column such as credit_limit or tenant_id, because the new field is writable by default. An allowlist fails closed: a new column is neither writable nor returned until someone adds it to an input or response type on purpose. Tests can lock this in by asserting each endpoint’s exact writable and returned fields for each role.

questions.prompt: A sign-up handler runs User.create(req.body). The users table has email, password_hash, role and email_verified. What can an attacker do?

choices.label: Sign up already verified, or as an admin
Read the password hashes of other users
Inject SQL through the email address
Nothing, as the ORM checks column types

questions.explanation: a: correct, any column named in the body is set, so "role": "admin" and "email_verified": true go straight in. b: that is over-exposure in responses, a different bug; this handler only writes. c: ORMs send values as parameters, so this is not an injection path. d: type checks pass happily, because "admin" is a valid string and true a valid boolean.

questions.prompt: A credit_limit column is added to users. Which design keeps it safe from client writes without anyone remembering to protect it?

choices.label: A denylist of fields clients may not set
An input type that lists the writable fields
Leaving the field out of the web form
A database trigger that logs every change

questions.explanation: a: the denylist was written before the column existed, so the new field is writable by default. b: correct, a field becomes writable only when someone adds it to the input type on purpose. c: anyone can send fields the form does not show. d: a log records the abuse after it has happened instead of preventing it.

questions.prompt: GET /users/42 returns the full user row, and the app shows only the name and avatar. What is the main problem?

choices.label: None, because the app hides the other fields
The response takes longer than it needs to
Anyone can read the hidden fields in the JSON
The client has to cache more than it needs

questions.explanation: a: hiding a field in the interface is not access control. b: larger responses are slower, but that is a side effect. c: correct, the raw response can be read with any HTTP client or the browser’s network tab, password hash and all. d: extra caching is a minor cost next to leaking private fields.

questions.prompt: A marketplace’s order list for buyers embeds each order’s seller object, serialised whole. What is most likely to leak?

choices.label: The seller’s phone number and internal notes
The buyer’s own delivery address
Each order’s price and current status
The seller’s public shop name and rating

questions.explanation: a: correct, the whole seller row carries private contact details and staff notes that buyers should never see. b: the buyer is entitled to their own address. c: price and status are meant to be shown on the order. d: the shop name and rating are public by design.

questions.prompt: A PATCH body contains a field the endpoint does not accept. Which handling is the safest default?

choices.label: Keep it in a JSON “extras” column for later
Copy it onto the model if a column matches
Reject with 400, or drop it and log it
Accept it silently, in production only

questions.explanation: a: storing unvetted fields invites someone to start trusting them later. b: that is mass assignment. c: correct, rejecting catches client bugs and probing early, and dropping with a log suits APIs that must tolerate newer clients; either way the field never reaches the model. d: behaving differently in production hides the problem where it matters most.

questions.prompt: Order how an update endpoint handles a request body.

items.label: Reject or drop fields the type does not accept
Apply those fields to the model and save it
Parse the body into the endpoint’s input type
Map the result to the response type for this caller
Check which accepted fields this caller may change

questions.explanation: Shape first, so nothing unexpected reaches later steps; authorise per field; write; then build the response from an explicit shape rather than the model.

questions.prompt: A list endpoint returns 50 users per page. A full serialised row is about 2 KB, and the public shape about 200 bytes. How many KB per page does returning the public shape save?
assumptions: 2 KB per full row, 200 bytes per public shape
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 100 KB falls to 10 KB, a 90% cut; at a million page views a day that is about 90 GB a day of data that should never have left the server.

flashcards.back: Copying a request body onto a model, so a caller can set fields like role or email_verified.

flashcards.front: Allowlist or denylist for writable fields?
flashcards.back: Allowlist: a new column stays unwritable until someone adds it on purpose.
A response type per view and role; never serialise the whole row.

sources.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

mechanism.title: How a handler decides which fields go in and out
steps: Each endpoint defines an input type: the exact fields it accepts, with their types and limits. Parsing the body into that type is the first step, and nothing else from the body reaches the model. Create and update usually need different types, because fields like an email may be set once and changed only through a verified flow.

Unknown fields are rejected with a 400 that names them, or dropped and logged; the choice is made once per API. Rejecting catches client bugs and probing early, while dropping makes it easier for older servers to accept newer clients. Either way, they are never copied.

Field-level authorisation follows. Some fields are writable only by certain roles or in certain states, such as a listing’s price only by its seller and only before it is published. Sensitive changes, such as a role or an email address, go through dedicated endpoints with their own checks and audit records.

The handler updates the model from the input type explicitly, field by field or through a mapping, never from the raw body. Server-owned fields, such as id, tenant_id, created_by, timestamps and balances, are set only by server code.

On the way out, the model is mapped to a response type for the caller’s view: public, owner or admin. Lists and nested objects use the same shapes, so a seller embedded in an order uses the public seller shape. Tests assert the exact field sets per endpoint and role, so a new column cannot slip out unnoticed.

useWhen: Any create or update endpoint backed by an ORM or a document store.
APIs whose responses are read by public or third-party clients.
avoidWhen: Avoid binding request bodies directly to database models.
Avoid denylists of forbidden fields, and returning whole rows.

rows: Bind the whole body to the model
Any caller can change privileges or state
A gap every time the schema grows
Input and response types per endpoint

numbers.title: What over-exposure costs on a list page
assumptions: Full row serialised: about 2 KB each
steps: Full rows: 50 × 2 KB = 100 KB per page.
Public shape: 50 × 200 bytes = 10 KB per page.
Saving: 90 KB per page, 90% of the payload.
At 1 million page views a day: about 90 GB a day of data, some of it private, that never needed to leave the server.
numbers.result: Explicit response shapes are first a security control; smaller, faster responses are a welcome side effect.

india.title: GitHub’s public-key form, 2012
india.label: Public incident, simplified
india.body: In March 2012 a user exploited GitHub’s public-key update form by adding a user id field to the request (CVE-2012-2055). The server code passed every submitted attribute to the update, so his SSH key was attached to the account of a major open-source project’s organisation, and he used it to push a file to that project’s repository. GitHub’s post-mortem named the root cause as a failure to check incoming form parameters, the mass-assignment vulnerability; it rolled out a fix about an hour after the attack and audited its codebase for other instances. The web framework involved later made an explicit allowlist of permitted fields the standard way to accept input.

pitfalls.trap: “The front end only sends the fields in the form.”
pitfalls.say: “Anyone can send any JSON, so I’d parse into an input type that accepts only the writable fields.”

pitfalls.trap: “The client ignores fields it doesn’t display.”
pitfalls.say: “The raw JSON is readable by anyone, so I’d return a response shape per role.”

takeaways: Never bind a request body straight onto a model.
Allowlist writable fields per endpoint and role; reject or drop the rest.
Return a response type per view, never the whole row.
Test the exact field sets, so new columns stay private by default.

interactive.title: A new column meets a denylist
interactive.prompt: A handler updates users with every key in the request body except role and is_admin. A developer adds a credit_limit column. What happens next?

choices.label: Any user can raise their own credit limit
choices.feedback: Right: the denylist was written before credit_limit existed, so the new column is writable by default.

choices.label: Updates fail until the field is listed somewhere
choices.feedback: That is how an allowlist behaves; a denylist lets new fields straight through.

choices.label: Only admins can change it, as with role
choices.feedback: Nothing ties credit_limit to the role check; only the two named fields are blocked.

interactive.reveal: Allowlists fail closed. Write an input type for each endpoint, and add a field to it only when that caller should control it.

seeAlso.why: Untrusted input: validating what arrives before it reaches the model
Field-level checks are authorisation applied to individual properties
Explicit response types mean a new column never reaches the API by accident

title: Long-Running Operations in APIs
objectives: Accept slow work with 202 Accepted and a status resource the client can poll
Keep polling cheap and retries safe with Retry-After, callbacks and idempotency keys
Support cancellation, failure states and expiry of operations and their results

cards.title: Hand back a ticket, not a held connection
cards.body: Generating a 2 GB export can take four minutes. Holding the HTTP request open that long fails in ordinary ways: proxies and load balancers close idle connections (60 seconds is a common default), mobile networks drop, and every waiting request holds a server connection. Instead, accept the work, queue it and reply 202 Accepted with a Location header such as /operations/op_81. The client polls that URL until the operation finishes, then fetches the result.

cards.title: Life of an operation
cards.body: The status resource is the record of where the work stands.
steps: POST /exports with an Idempotency-Key; reply 202 and Location: /operations/op_81
A worker picks it up: status moves from queued to running, with progress
The client polls the status URL, waiting as long as Retry-After says
Finished: status done with a link to the result, or failed with an error
The operation and its result expire after a stated time, such as 7 days

cards.title: Worked example: what polling costs
cards.body: 50,000 exports a day, each running about 4 minutes. If clients poll every second, that is 240 polls each, or 12M status requests a day for 50,000 jobs. Polling every 10 seconds cuts it to 1.2M. Backing off instead (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s, then every 30 s) needs only about a dozen polls per job, around 600,000 a day. Send Retry-After on each status reply so the server, not the client, sets the pace.

cards.title: Callbacks alongside the status URL
cards.body: A webhook on completion saves clients from polling at all, but webhooks get lost: the receiver is down, a firewall blocks it, or a retry gives up. Keep the status URL as the record and treat the callback as a hint that it is worth checking now. Sign callbacks so the receiver can tell they came from you, and include only the operation id, so a forged or replayed callback reveals nothing.

cards.title: Trap: a retried POST starts a second job
cards.body: The client’s POST times out before the 202 arrives, so it retries, and two exports run. Require an Idempotency-Key on the POST and return the same operation id for a repeat. Also plan for the unhappy endings: a cancel request moves the operation to cancelling and then cancelled, workers check for it between chunks, a worker that stops sending heartbeats gets its operation retried or marked failed, and done, failed and cancelled are final.

questions.prompt: An endpoint starts a report that takes about 3 minutes to build. What should the first response be?

choices.label: 200 OK, sent once the report finishes
202 Accepted with a status URL
201 Created with an empty report body
504 Gateway Timeout, asking for a retry

questions.explanation: a: the connection must stay open for 3 minutes, and proxies may close it first. b: correct, the work is accepted and the client gets somewhere to check on it. c: 201 says the resource exists now, which it does not. d: a 504 tells the client something failed, and a retry would start the work again.

questions.prompt: How should a server tell clients how often to poll an operation’s status?

choices.label: Close the connection when a client polls too soon
Reply 429 to every poll until the work is done
Document a fixed 1-second interval for all
Send a Retry-After header on each status reply

questions.explanation: a: closing connections looks like a network error and invites fast retries. b: 429 to well-behaved clients turns normal polling into errors. c: a fixed 1-second interval creates heavy load for long jobs. d: correct, the server can lengthen the wait for long jobs or under load.

questions.prompt: A status URL says “running” for hours because the worker crashed. What fixes this?

choices.label: Clients poll more often so they notice sooner
A heartbeat timeout that retries or marks it failed
The status endpoint returns 500 while a job runs
Status records are deleted after one hour

questions.explanation: a: polling faster just reads the same stale status more often. b: correct, a worker that stops heartbeating has its operation retried or moved to failed, so clients get a final state. c: a 500 tells the client the status service broke, not the job. d: deleting the record leaves the client with a 404 and no explanation.

questions.prompt: A POST /exports times out before the 202 arrives, and the client retries with the same Idempotency-Key. What should happen?

choices.label: A second export starts under a new id
The server replies 409 with no id
The server returns the same operation id
The first export is cancelled and restarted

questions.explanation: a: that is the duplicate the key exists to prevent. b: a 409 leaves the client unable to find the job it started. c: correct, the client gets the status URL of the export that is already running. d: restarting wastes the work already done.

questions.prompt: Why keep a status URL when you also send a completion webhook?

choices.label: Webhooks cannot carry the result’s location
Status URLs are needed to authenticate
Clients must poll before a webhook is sent
Webhooks can be lost; the URL is the record

questions.explanation: a: a webhook can carry a link, but it may never arrive. b: authentication is separate from how status is reported. c: clients that get webhooks need not poll at all on the happy path. d: correct, a client that missed the callback can still find out the result.

questions.prompt: Order a long-running export from the client’s side.

items.label: See status done with a result link
POST with an Idempotency-Key
Download the result before it expires
Poll, waiting as long as Retry-After says
Receive 202 and the status URL

questions.explanation: The key makes the first step safe to retry, and the expiry on the result is why the last step has a deadline.

questions.prompt: 30,000 operations a day each run about 5 minutes, and clients poll every 2 seconds. Roughly how many status polls is that per day?
assumptions: Each operation is polled from start to finish
questions.explanation: Design implication: a Retry-After of 30 s cuts this to 300,000 polls a day, and a completion webhook cuts it to almost none for clients that can receive one.

flashcards.back: 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing at a status resource.
Retry-After on each status reply, client backoff, and optional webhooks.
done (with a result link), failed (with an error) or cancelled.

mechanism.title: How an API runs work that outlasts a request
steps: The client sends the request with an Idempotency-Key. The server validates it, checks the key and stores a new operation record, with an id, a status of queued, the request parameters and an expiry time, in the same transaction that enqueues the job. It replies 202 Accepted, a Location header pointing at /operations/{id}, and a small body with the id and status. If the key was seen before, it returns the existing operation instead.

A worker takes the job, marks the operation running and updates progress as it goes, such as rows exported or a percentage. It sends heartbeats while it works. A supervisor looks for running operations whose heartbeat has stopped, then retries them if the work is idempotent or marks them failed with a reason, so no client polls a dead job forever.

Clients poll the status URL. Each reply says the status and carries a Retry-After header, short at first and longer for jobs known to be slow or when the system is busy. Clients back off between polls and stop at a final state. Clients that can receive webhooks register a callback URL and get a signed notification on completion, but the status resource remains the record they can always check.

The operation ends in one final state. done includes a link to the result, often a short-lived signed URL to a file in object storage. failed includes a machine-readable error code and a message. cancelled follows a cancel request: the API marks the operation cancelling, the worker checks for that between chunks, cleans up and marks it cancelled. A final state never changes again.

Operations and results do not live forever. The API documents how long they are kept, for example 7 days, after which the status URL returns 404 or 410 and the result file is deleted. A cleanup job enforces this. The documented limit lets clients plan, and it stops storage from growing without bound as millions of old exports pile up.

useWhen: Exports, reports, media processing and other work that takes more than a few seconds.
Requests whose duration varies widely and can exceed proxy timeouts.
avoidWhen: Avoid it for work that reliably finishes within about a second; a direct reply is simpler.
Avoid polling every second with no Retry-After; it creates load out of nothing.

numbers.title: Held connections versus a ticket
assumptions: Each export takes 240 s to build
steps: Synchronous: by Little’s law, concurrent requests = arrival rate × time = 1 × 240 = 240 connections held open.
Each held connection also needs a worker waiting on it, and any proxy with a 60 s idle timeout will cut them first.
Asynchronous: 1 × 0.05 s = 0.05 connections busy on average for the requests themselves.
The 240 builds still run, but on queue workers whose number you choose, not on request threads.
numbers.result: A ticket moves long work off the request path, where it no longer holds connections or depends on proxy timeouts.

india.title: Bank statements and tax data exports
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: an accounting app lets a firm download twelve months of transactions for all its clients ahead of the tax filing deadline. The export can take several minutes and many firms ask in the same week. The API returns 202 with a status URL, sends Retry-After of 15 seconds and then longer, and notifies the firm’s webhook when the file is ready. The result link expires after seven days, and a retried request with the same idempotency key returns the export already running instead of starting another.

pitfalls.trap: “We just raised the load balancer timeout to 10 minutes.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d return 202 with a status URL, so long work does not depend on any proxy timeout.”

pitfalls.trap: “The webhook tells them when it is done.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d keep a status URL as the record too, because callbacks can be lost.”

takeaways: Reply 202 with a status URL for work that outlasts a request.
Use Retry-After and backoff to keep polling cheap; add signed callbacks.
Require an idempotency key so a retried POST does not start a second job.
Define final states, heartbeats, cancellation and expiry.

interactive.title: A slow PDF behind a load balancer
interactive.prompt: An endpoint builds PDFs synchronously. Most take 20 s, but large ones take 90 s. The load balancer closes connections idle for 60 s. What do users with large PDFs see?

choices.label: A timeout error while the server keeps building the PDF
choices.feedback: Right: the load balancer gives up at 60 s, but the work continues and its result has nowhere to go.

choices.label: The PDF, just after a longer wait
choices.feedback: The connection is closed at 60 s, before the reply exists.

choices.label: A 202 response that the load balancer adds for them
choices.feedback: Load balancers do not convert slow requests into asynchronous ones.

interactive.reveal: The user gets an error, retries and starts a second 90-second build. Return 202 with a status URL, build in a worker, and the timeout stops mattering.

seeAlso.why: The work behind a 202 runs as a background job on a queue
Idempotency keys make the starting POST safe to retry
Completion callbacks are webhooks and should be signed and retried the same way
Account deletion across services is a long-running operation with a status

title: Testing a Service: Unit, Integration and Contract Tests
objectives: Match unit, integration, contract and end-to-end tests to the risks they catch
Test data access against a real database instead of a mock that agrees with you
Keep tests fast and repeatable by controlling time, randomness and shared state

cards.title: Match the test to the risk
cards.body: Unit tests check pure logic, such as a price or tax calculation, in milliseconds. Integration tests run your code against real dependencies, above all the database, and catch wrong SQL, missing migrations and violated constraints, in about a second each. Contract tests check that your API still gives each consumer the fields and types it relies on. End-to-end tests drive a whole user journey across services; they are slow and fail for unrelated reasons, so keep a few for the critical paths.

cards.title: Worked example: the bug a mock agreed with
cards.body: A sign-up handler relies on a unique constraint on email and turns the database’s unique-violation error into a 409. The unit test mocks the repository to “throw a duplicate error”, and passes. In production the driver reports the violation with a different error code from the one the handler checks, so users get a 500. Only a test against a real database, started fresh in a container and migrated with the real migrations, exercises the constraint and the actual error the driver returns.

cards.title: A consumer-driven contract test
cards.body: Each consumer states what it relies on; the provider checks it on every build.
steps: The consumer records the requests it sends and the response fields it reads
Those expectations are published as a contract file
The provider’s build replays each request against the real provider
A removed field or changed type fails the provider’s build, before release
Both sides deploy knowing they still agree

cards.title: Flaky tests come from hidden inputs
cards.body: A test that sometimes fails usually reads something it does not control: the clock, random numbers, test order, data left by another test, or a real network call. Pass in a clock the test can set, seed random generators, give each test its own data (a rolled-back transaction or unique ids), and wait for a condition rather than a fixed sleep. Flakiness adds up: 400 tests that each fail 0.5% of the time make 1 − 0.995^400 ≈ 86% of runs go red.

cards.title: Trap: chasing coverage instead of risks
cards.body: 90% line coverage can still miss the concurrent double booking, the migration that locks a table, the timeout path and the retried request. Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether the failure cases were checked. List the ways the service can fail, such as a dependency timeout, a duplicate request, a partial write or a bad input, and write a test for each one.

questions.prompt: Which test best catches a wrong tax calculation for a cart?

choices.label: An end-to-end test run through the browser
A contract test against the payments API
A unit test of the price function
A load test at expected peak traffic

questions.explanation: a: it could catch it, slowly, and a failure would not say which part was wrong. b: a contract checks the shape of calls between services, not the arithmetic. c: correct, pure logic is best tested directly with many cases, including rounding edges. d: load tests measure capacity, not correctness.

questions.prompt: A test with a mocked database passes, but production returns 500 on duplicate sign-ups. What would have caught it?

choices.label: More unit tests around the mocked handler
A higher line-coverage threshold in CI
Running the same suite twice in a row
An integration test on a real database

questions.explanation: a: more tests against the same mock repeat the same wrong assumption. b: the lines already ran; coverage cannot see the wrong error mapping. c: a deterministic test passes twice just as easily. d: correct, a real database raises the real constraint error and exposes the mapping bug.

questions.prompt: A provider team renames a JSON field. With consumer-driven contract tests, what fails first?

choices.label: The provider’s own build
The consumer’s production traffic
The consumer’s unit tests
A nightly end-to-end run

questions.explanation: a: correct, the provider replays each consumer’s expectations and the missing field fails its build before release. b: that is what happens without contracts. c: the consumer’s tests use its own stub of the provider, which still has the old field. d: an end-to-end run might notice later, if it covers that field.

questions.prompt: A test checks that a token “expires in 1 hour” and fails a few times a week, always near midnight. What is the right fix?

choices.label: Retry the test up to three times in CI
Inject a clock the test can control
Raise the test’s timeout to one hour
Run the suite only during working hours

questions.explanation: a: retries hide the flakiness and the bug it may point to. b: correct, the code reads time from a clock the test sets, so the result no longer depends on when it runs. c: the failure is about dates, not slowness. d: avoiding midnight hides a real date-boundary bug that users will hit.

questions.prompt: Tests pass one at a time but fail when the suite runs in random order. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The CI machine has too little memory
A race inside the test framework itself
Shared state left behind by another test
The database is too slow under parallel load

questions.explanation: a: memory pressure fails tests regardless of order. b: possible but rare; suspect your own tests first. c: correct, one test leaves data or settings that another depends on or trips over; isolate each test’s data. d: slowness causes timeouts, which do not depend on order.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an isolated database integration test.

items.label: Begin a transaction for this test
Roll back so the next test starts clean
Start a fresh database, for example in a container
Run the code and check the rows it wrote
Apply the real migrations

questions.explanation: Real migrations prove the schema, and the rollback gives every test the same starting point without rebuilding the database.

questions.prompt: A suite has 300 tests and each fails at random 0.2% of the time, independently. Roughly what percent of runs fail at least once?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: nearly half the runs go red with no real bug, so people stop trusting the suite; each flaky test is worth fixing.

flashcards.front: What does an integration test catch that a unit test misses?
flashcards.back: Wrong SQL, missing migrations and real constraint errors from the actual database.
Consumers publish what they rely on; the provider’s build checks it before release.
Time, randomness, test order, shared data and real network calls.

sources.title: Martin Fowler: The Practical Test Pyramid
Martin Fowler: Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests

mechanism.title: How a backend test suite is put together
steps: Start from risks, not layers. List what can go wrong: business rules computed wrongly, queries that return the wrong rows, a migration that breaks old data, an API change that breaks a consumer, a dependency that times out, a request that is retried. Each risk points at the cheapest kind of test that can catch it, and that kind is the one to write.

Pure logic gets unit tests: functions that take values and return values, with no database or network. Keep business rules in such functions where you can, because they can then be tested with hundreds of cases, including rounding edges and empty inputs, in well under a second. Mocks belong at the boundary of this code, and only for things that are slow or outside your control.

Data access gets integration tests against the real database engine, the same version as production, started fresh for the test run, often in a container, and built with the real migrations. Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, or uses its own unique ids, so tests do not see each other’s data. These tests catch the bugs mocks cannot: SQL errors, constraint errors, wrong isolation assumptions and slow queries.

Service boundaries get contract tests. Each consumer records the requests it makes and the parts of the response it reads; the provider’s pipeline replays them on every build. A provider can then remove a field nobody reads without fear, and is stopped from removing one that someone does. A small number of end-to-end tests cover the journeys that would cost the most to break, such as sign-up and checkout.

Everything runs on every change, so speed and determinism matter. Time, randomness and identifiers are passed in so tests can fix them. Waits poll for a condition with a timeout instead of sleeping. Tests that turn out to be flaky are quarantined and fixed quickly, because a suite that fails at random teaches people to ignore red builds, and then real failures get ignored too.

useWhen: Any service that will be changed by more than one person over time.
Services with consumers in other teams, where contracts prevent surprise breakage.
avoidWhen: Avoid mocking the database to test queries; the mock agrees with whatever you assumed.
Avoid a large end-to-end suite as the main safety net; it is slow and fails for unrelated reasons.

numbers.title: A CI budget of 10 minutes
assumptions: 2,000 unit tests at about 5 ms each
200 integration tests at about 300 ms each
20 end-to-end tests at about 30 s each
steps: Integration: 200 × 0.3 s = 60 s.
End-to-end: 20 × 30 s = 600 s, ten times the other two combined.
Total 670 s, about 11 minutes on one worker; split over 4 workers, about 2.8 minutes.
numbers.result: End-to-end tests dominate the time even when there are few of them. Keep each one for a journey that really needs it, and push the rest down to integration and unit tests.

india.title: A payments integration tested before go-live
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a team adding UPI payments to an app tests its fee and refund arithmetic with unit tests, runs integration tests against a real database to check that a repeated payment callback is rejected by a unique constraint, and runs contract tests against the payment provider’s published sandbox behaviour. A handful of end-to-end tests cover pay, refund and a timed-out payment. The flakiest test turned out to depend on the time of day and was fixed by passing in a clock.

pitfalls.trap: “We have 90% coverage, so it is well tested.”
pitfalls.say: “Coverage shows which lines ran; I’d check that each failure mode, like timeouts and retries, has a test.”

pitfalls.trap: “We mock the database so tests are fast.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d mock it in unit tests but run data access against a real database, since that is where the bugs are.”

takeaways: Pick the cheapest test that can catch each risk.
Test queries and migrations against a real database.
Contract tests stop breaking API changes before release.
Control time, randomness and shared data to keep tests repeatable.

interactive.title: A test plan for an orders service
interactive.prompt: Pick the best fit for these constraints.
setup: The orders service owns a relational database schema
Three other teams call its API
CI must finish in under 10 minutes

choices.label: Unit tests, real-database integration tests and consumer contracts
choices.feedback: Right: each risk is covered by the cheapest test that catches it, inside the time budget.

choices.label: A large end-to-end suite that runs all four services
choices.feedback: Catches cross-service breaks, but it is slow, fails for unrelated reasons and will not fit 10 minutes.

choices.label: Unit tests with a mocked database, for speed
choices.feedback: Fast, but SQL, migrations and constraints go untested, and API changes reach consumers unchecked.

interactive.reveal: Logic in unit tests, data access against a real database, and contracts for the three consumers cover the main risks in a few minutes. Add a handful of end-to-end tests for the journeys that would cost most to break.

seeAlso.why: These tests are the gates a CI/CD pipeline runs on every change
Contract tests are how you know an API change is still backward compatible
Schema compatibility checks are contract tests for messages and events
The front-end side of the same test pyramid: component, integration and end-to-end tests

title: Deleting Data Across a Service: Cascades, Tombstones and Workflows
objectives: Choose the ON DELETE action for each foreign key, and stage large deletes instead of one huge cascade
Run account deletion as a tracked workflow across services, with idempotent steps
Stop deleted data coming back through retries, replays, caches and offline sync

cards.title: What a foreign key does on delete
cards.body: ON DELETE CASCADE removes child rows with the parent; RESTRICT (or NO ACTION) refuses the delete while children exist; SET NULL keeps the child and clears the link. Choose per relationship: an order’s line items cascade with the order, a customer’s invoices restrict the delete until they are dealt with, and a comment’s author can become null (“deleted user”). Index every foreign-key column: PostgreSQL does not create that index for you, and without it each parent delete scans the whole child table.

cards.title: Worked example: deleting a workspace with 3 million rows
cards.body: DELETE FROM workspaces WHERE id = 42, with cascades to projects, tasks, comments and attachments, is one statement but one transaction over 3 million rows: locks held for minutes, a surge of write-ahead log, replicas falling behind, and if it times out, everything rolls back and starts again. Instead mark the workspace deleting, so the app hides it and refuses writes, then delete the children leaf-first in batches of a few thousand rows (comments, tasks, projects), and the workspace row last, when the cascades have nothing left to do. Files in object storage are outside the database, so the same job deletes them by prefix.

cards.title: Account deletion as a workflow
cards.body: Deletion has an id and a status, and it is finished only when every owner says so.
steps: Request accepted: the account is marked deleting and sign-in is blocked
A UserDeleted event is written to the outbox in the same transaction
Each service that owns data deletes or anonymises it and acknowledges
The workflow tracks each service’s status and retries failed steps
When all have acknowledged, the account becomes a tombstone and completion is recorded

cards.title: Tombstones stop data coming back
cards.body: Deleted data returns in quiet ways: a retried job re-creates a profile from a queued message, a cache refills from a lagging replica, an offline phone syncs its old copy, a replayed event rebuilds a read model. Keep a small tombstone, the id and when it was deleted with no personal data, and make writers, consumers and sync endpoints check it: an upsert for a tombstoned id is dropped, and sync answers with a delete marker. Keep tombstones for longer than any queue, cache or offline client can hold an old copy.

cards.title: Trap: “deleted” after one service says so
cards.body: If the API returns success as soon as it has deleted its own rows and fired an untracked event, a consumer that was down or has a bug leaves data behind, and nobody finds out. Treat deletion as a long-running operation: give it an id and a status, require every service that owns data to acknowledge, retry failed steps, and alert on any step stuck past the promised window. Each step must be idempotent, so deleting something already gone counts as success.

questions.prompt: Invoices reference customers, and accounting rules say invoices must be kept. Which ON DELETE action fits that foreign key?

choices.label: CASCADE, so invoices go with the customer
RESTRICT, so the delete waits for a decision
SET NULL, leaving invoices with no customer
No foreign key, so nothing ever blocks

questions.explanation: a: a cascade silently destroys records the business must keep. b: correct, the delete fails until code deals with the invoices on purpose, for example by anonymising the customer’s personal fields while keeping the invoice. c: invoices lose who was billed, which accounting still needs, and it happens without anyone deciding. d: without the constraint, invoices can point at customers that no longer exist.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, deleting one customer takes 40 seconds, though they have only 12 orders. orders.customer_id references customers with ON DELETE CASCADE. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: orders.customer_id has no index, so orders is scanned
CASCADE locks the entire orders table
The customers table needs a VACUUM first
Foreign keys are only checked at commit time

questions.explanation: a: correct, PostgreSQL indexes the referenced key but not the referencing column, so finding the 12 orders means reading the whole table. b: a cascade locks the child rows it deletes, not the table. c: dead rows can slow scans a little, but not into tens of seconds for one customer. d: when the check runs does not change how the child rows are found.
