questions.prompt: Deleting a workspace cascades to 3 million rows in one statement and keeps timing out. What is the better approach?

choices.label: Mark it deleting, then delete its children in batches
Run the same statement at night with no timeout
Drop the foreign keys so the delete runs instantly
Soft-delete the workspace and keep every row

questions.explanation: a: correct, short batch transactions keep locks brief and replicas close, the job can resume after a failure, and the deleting flag hides the workspace meanwhile. b: at night it still holds locks for minutes, floods replicas, and restarts from zero on any failure. c: the rows still have to be deleted, and the database stops protecting the links. d: hiding is not deleting, and the rows keep growing.

questions.prompt: A user was deleted, yet their profile reappears a day later after a queued “update profile” message was retried. What prevents this?

choices.label: A tombstone that consumers check before writing
A longer delay between retries on the queue
Running the deletion twice to make sure
Clearing the cache after every deletion

questions.explanation: a: correct, the consumer sees that the id was deleted and drops the upsert. b: the message still arrives eventually, whatever the delay. c: the late message can arrive after the second run too. d: the profile came back through a database write, not the cache.

questions.prompt: Account deletion publishes UserDeleted and the API reports “deleted” at once. The search service was down for an hour that day. What is the gap?

choices.label: Nothing records whether every service finished
The event should have been sent as an email
UserDeleted events can never be retried
The API should not publish any events at all

questions.explanation: a: correct, without a status per service nobody knows the search index still holds the user, so nothing retries or alerts. b: the delivery channel is not the problem; tracking is. c: events can be redelivered, but only if something notices the step failed. d: an event is a fine way to tell services, as long as their acknowledgements are tracked.

questions.prompt: Order how a service handles an account deletion across services.

items.label: Each owning service deletes or anonymises its data and acknowledges
Turn the account into a tombstone and record completion
Mark the account deleting and block sign-in
Retry and alert on any step that has not acknowledged
Write UserDeleted to the outbox in the same transaction

questions.explanation: Stop new activity first, publish reliably with the state change, collect acknowledgements, chase the stragglers, and only then declare the deletion complete.

questions.prompt: A job deletes a workspace’s 3 million child rows in batches of 2,000. Each batch takes 0.1 s, plus a 0.1 s pause before the next. How many minutes does it take?
assumptions: No other load on the table
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 5 minutes of short transactions is harmless, while one 3-million-row statement would hold its locks for the whole time and roll everything back on failure.

flashcards.back: Cascade parts of a thing, restrict records that must be kept, set null for links that may outlive the parent.
So retries, replays, caches and offline sync cannot bring deleted data back.
A tracked workflow: event through the outbox, an acknowledgement per service, retries and alerts until all are done.

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Saga pattern
OWASP: User Privacy Protection cheat sheet

mechanism.title: How a deletion travels through a service and its neighbours
steps: Every foreign key gets an explicit ON DELETE chosen by ownership: parts of a thing cascade, records with their own duties restrict, optional links set null. Every referencing column is indexed, so cascades and checks find children without scanning.

Large deletes are staged. The parent is marked deleting, hidden and read-only; a batch job deletes children leaf-first in short transactions with a checkpoint; the parent goes last. The same job removes what the database does not hold, such as files in object storage, keyed or prefixed by the parent’s id.

Deletion across services is a workflow with an id and a status. The owning service commits the deleting state and an outbox event in one transaction; each consumer deletes or anonymises idempotently and acknowledges; the coordinator retries, alerts when a step exceeds the promised window, and records completion.

Tombstones hold the id and deletion time, without personal data, for as long as any queue, cache, replica or offline client could still carry an old copy. Writers check them, sync endpoints return delete markers, and event consumers treat a tombstoned id as final.

Exceptions are designed in, not bolted on. Records that a law or contract requires you to keep, often invoices and payment records, are anonymised rather than deleted; a legal hold pauses a deletion; and the completion record lists what was kept and why, without the deleted data itself. Which records must be kept, and for how long, depends on the jurisdiction, so the rules come from legal advice, not from engineering.

useWhen: Account and workspace deletion, tenant offboarding, and removing objects with many children.
Systems where several services, caches or devices hold copies of the same records.
avoidWhen: Avoid one cascading DELETE over millions of rows in a live transaction.
Avoid fire-and-forget deletion events with no acknowledgement or status.

rows: Parts of the parent: line items, a post’s comments
The delete fails while children exist
Records with their own duties: invoices, payouts

numbers.title: Why a deletion needs tracking
assumptions: 12 services hold data for each user
Each finishes its step on the first try 99.5% of the time
steps: All 12 succeed first time: 0.995^12 ≈ 0.942.
So about 5.8% of deletions have at least one failed step.
2,000 × 5.8% ≈ 117 deletions a day need a retry.
Without a status per step, each of those silently leaves data behind.
numbers.result: Small failure rates add up across many services. Track each step, retry automatically, and alert only on what retries cannot fix.

india.title: Deleting a workspace in a project-management app
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a project-management app let admins delete a workspace, and the first version ran one cascading DELETE. Large customers’ deletions timed out and rolled back, and smaller ones still left files in object storage and documents in the search index. The rebuild marked the workspace deleting, ran a resumable batch job leaf-first, published WorkspaceDeleted through the outbox, and tracked acknowledgements from search, files and billing. Billing anonymised invoices instead of deleting them. Tombstones stopped an offline mobile client from re-uploading tasks a week later.

pitfalls.trap: “Just put ON DELETE CASCADE everywhere.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d choose per relationship: cascade parts, restrict what we must keep, and batch big deletes.”

pitfalls.trap: “We publish an event, so every service deletes the user.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d track each service’s acknowledgement, retry failures, and keep a tombstone so late messages cannot recreate the data.”

takeaways: Choose ON DELETE per relationship, and index every foreign-key column.
Stage large deletes: mark, delete children in batches, then the parent.
Run cross-service deletion as a tracked, idempotent workflow.
Keep tombstones so retries, caches and sync cannot bring data back.

interactive.title: An offline phone syncs a deleted note
interactive.prompt: A user deletes a note on their laptop, and the server hard-deletes the row, keeping no record. Their phone, offline for a week, then syncs its copy, which includes the note. The sync endpoint upserts every note it receives. What happens?

choices.label: The note is recreated on the server and the laptop
choices.feedback: Right: with no trace of the delete, the server cannot tell an old copy from a new note.

choices.label: The server rejects the note as deleted
choices.feedback: Only if it had kept a tombstone; the hard delete left nothing to compare against.

choices.label: The phone deletes its own copy during sync
choices.feedback: The phone needs a delete marker from the server, and none exists.

interactive.reveal: Keep a tombstone with the id and deletion time, have sync send delete markers and drop upserts for tombstoned ids, and expire tombstones only after the longest time a client may stay offline.

seeAlso.why: Large deletes run as resumable batch jobs with checkpoints and throttling
A deletion request is a long-running operation with an id and a status
The deletion event leaves through an outbox written in the same transaction
Minimising and pseudonymising the personal data that deletion workflows have to find

title: Batch Jobs Over Millions of Rows: Chunking, Checkpoints and Throttling
objectives: Process a large table in key-ordered chunks with a saved checkpoint
Make each chunk idempotent so a crashed job can resume safely
Throttle batch work so live traffic and replicas keep up

cards.title: One giant transaction does not scale
cards.body: Backfilling a new column on 50M rows with a single UPDATE holds locks for a long time, writes one enormous transaction to the log, makes replicas fall far behind, and if it fails at 90% it rolls back everything and starts again. The same job run as thousands of small transactions keeps each lock brief, lets replicas keep pace, and turns a failure into losing one chunk instead of hours of work.

cards.title: Key-ordered chunks with a checkpoint
cards.body: Each pass picks up exactly where the last one stopped.
steps: Read the checkpoint: last id done = 1,240,000
Select the next 2,000 rows WHERE id > 1,240,000 ORDER BY id
Process them and write the results in one short transaction
Save the chunk’s last id as the new checkpoint in that same transaction
Pause if replica lag or live latency is over its limit, then repeat

cards.title: Worked example: how long a backfill takes
cards.body: 50M rows in chunks of 2,000 is 25,000 chunks. At 150 ms per chunk that is 3,750 s, about an hour; adding a 100 ms pause between chunks makes it 25,000 × 0.25 s = 6,250 s, about 1.7 hours. Selecting chunks with OFFSET instead would make each chunk skip all earlier rows: chunk 20,000 reads past 40M rows before returning 2,000. Key-ordered chunks start from the index every time, so the last chunk costs the same as the first.

cards.title: Idempotent chunks make restarts dull
cards.body: A job can crash after writing a chunk but before saving its checkpoint, unless both happen in one transaction, and then that chunk runs again. Make the work safe to repeat: set values computed from the row (SET total = price × qty) rather than adding to them, add a condition such as WHERE total IS NULL, and use upserts with unique keys. For side effects such as sending emails, record a per-row sent marker in the same transaction as the work.

cards.title: Trap: running flat out against the primary
cards.body: A backfill running at full speed can take the primary database’s disk and CPU, so live p99 latency rises and replicas fall behind, which users see as their own changes disappearing for a while. Throttle it: a fixed rate, pauses whenever replica lag passes a limit such as 1 second, backing off when live latency rises, and running in quieter hours. A job that takes a day without anyone noticing beats one that takes an hour and pages the on-call engineer.

questions.prompt: Why run a 50M-row backfill in chunks of a few thousand rows?

choices.label: Chunked updates use less disk in total
Short transactions keep locks and lag small
Chunks let the job skip rows it does not need
Smaller chunks reduce the total work done

questions.explanation: a: the total data written is about the same. b: correct, each transaction is brief, replicas keep up, and a failure loses only one chunk. c: which rows are touched depends on the WHERE clause, not the chunking. d: chunking adds a little overhead; its value is safety, not less work.

questions.prompt: Why select each chunk with WHERE id > last_id rather than OFFSET?

choices.label: OFFSET returns rows in a random order
OFFSET cannot be combined with ORDER BY
Each chunk starts from the index, not by skipping
Keyset queries take no locks of any kind

questions.explanation: a: with ORDER BY, OFFSET is ordered too; its cost is the problem. b: OFFSET is normally used with ORDER BY. c: correct, a keyset query seeks straight to the next key, while OFFSET reads and discards every earlier row, so late chunks get slower and slower. d: the writes in each chunk still take row locks.

questions.prompt: A job commits each chunk, then saves its checkpoint in a separate transaction, and crashes between the two. What happens on restart?

choices.label: The last chunk is skipped
The last chunk is processed again
The whole job restarts from row one
The database rolls back both writes

questions.explanation: a: the checkpoint still points before the chunk, so nothing is skipped. b: correct, the work is redone, which is safe only if the chunk is idempotent; saving the checkpoint in the same transaction avoids it. c: the checkpoint is only one chunk behind. d: the chunk’s transaction had already committed.

questions.prompt: Which chunk update is safe to run twice?

choices.label: SET total = total + price × qty
SET visits = visits + 1
INSERT a copy of each row into an archive with no key
SET total = price × qty

questions.explanation: a: running it twice adds the amount twice. b: every rerun increments again. c: without a unique key, a rerun inserts duplicates. d: correct, it sets the value from the row itself, so a second run writes the same result.

questions.prompt: During a backfill, replica lag climbs to 40 s and users stop seeing their own changes. What should the job do?

choices.label: Pause until lag is under a limit, then resume
Use bigger chunks to finish sooner
Switch to one large transaction
Keep going; the lag clears when it ends

questions.explanation: a: correct, lag-aware throttling lets replicas catch up and keeps the job running safely. b: bigger chunks make each transaction heavier and lag worse. c: one huge transaction is the worst case for replicas. d: users suffer for the whole run, which may be hours.

questions.prompt: Order one pass of a resumable batch job.

items.label: Write the results in a short transaction
Check replica lag and pause if needed
Read the last saved checkpoint
Save the chunk’s last key as the checkpoint
Fetch the next chunk after it, in key order

questions.explanation: The checkpoint brackets the work: read it first, advance it only after the chunk is written, then let the throttle decide when the next pass starts.

questions.prompt: A job updates 12M rows in chunks of 4,000, and each chunk takes 0.3 s including its pause. About how many minutes does it run?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with OFFSET-based chunks the late chunks would scan millions of skipped rows each, and the same job could take many hours.

flashcards.back: Short transactions keep locks, log size and replica lag small, and failures cheap.
WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n, so every chunk starts from the index.

flashcards.front: How is a batch kept from hurting live traffic?
flashcards.back: Throttle on replica lag and live latency, with pauses and a rate limit.

mechanism.title: How a resumable batch job walks a big table
steps: The job walks the table in primary-key order, or in any indexed, unique order. Each pass selects the next n rows after the last key it finished, with a condition such as WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 2000. Because the database seeks straight to that key in the index, every chunk costs about the same, whether it is the first or the twenty-thousandth.

Each chunk is processed and written in one short transaction. The chunk size is chosen so a transaction takes well under a second, typically a few hundred to a few thousand rows, and tuned by measuring. Small enough to keep locks brief and replicas close behind; large enough that per-transaction overhead does not dominate.

The checkpoint, the last key finished, is saved in a small job table, ideally in the same transaction as the chunk’s writes, so the two can never disagree. On restart the job reads the checkpoint and continues. If the checkpoint is saved separately, a crash can repeat one chunk, so the chunk’s work must be idempotent anyway: set values rather than increment them, filter for rows not yet done, and upsert on unique keys.

Between chunks the job checks the health of the system it is loading: replica lag, the primary’s CPU or I/O, and the p99 latency of live queries. If any is over its limit, it sleeps and checks again. A rate cap, a time-of-day window and a kill switch that stops it within one chunk give operators control without killing processes.

The job reports progress: the checkpoint, rows done, rows per second and an estimated finish time. It ends with a verification step, such as counting rows still not done, which must be zero. For schema changes the usual order is to add the new column, deploy code that writes it for new rows, backfill old rows with the job, verify, and only then make the column required or start reading from it.

useWhen: Backfills, data migrations, re-encryption, recomputing derived columns.
Any job touching more rows than one transaction should hold.
avoidWhen: Avoid OFFSET to page through a big table; late pages get slower and slower.
Avoid running batch work flat out on the primary during peak hours.

rows: Keyset chunks with checkpoint and throttle

numbers.title: OFFSET versus keyset over a large table
assumptions: OFFSET reads and discards every earlier row
steps: Keyset: each chunk reads about 2,000 rows, so about 50M row reads in total.
OFFSET: chunk k first skips (k − 1) × 2,000 rows; on average about 25M skipped rows per chunk.
Total for OFFSET: about 25,000 × 25M ≈ 6 × 10^11 row reads, roughly 12,500 times the keyset total.
Even at millions of rows read per second, that is days of extra work.
numbers.result: Key-ordered chunks keep a long job’s cost linear in the table size; OFFSET makes it quadratic.

india.title: Backfilling a column in a large payments table
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a payments company adds a normalised merchant category to a table of several hundred million transactions. The team adds a nullable column, deploys code that fills it for new rows, then runs a backfill in chunks of 2,000 by primary key, saving the checkpoint with each chunk and pausing whenever replica lag passes one second. The job runs for most of a day at a rate nobody notices. A final count of rows still null confirms it finished before the column is made required.

pitfalls.trap: “We will run one UPDATE over the weekend.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d chunk it by key with a checkpoint, so it can pause, resume and never lag the replicas.”

pitfalls.trap: “If it crashes we will rerun it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d make each chunk idempotent, so reruns are safe and it resumes from the checkpoint.”

takeaways: Walk big tables in key order, in short transactions.
Save a checkpoint with each chunk so the job resumes, not restarts.
Make chunk work idempotent: set rather than increment.
Throttle on replica lag and live latency.

interactive.title: Backfilling 80M rows on a live database
interactive.prompt: Pick the best fit for these constraints.
setup: 80M rows on the primary database need a new column filled
Users read from replicas and expect their changes within 2 s
The job may take a day

choices.label: Keyset chunks with a checkpoint, paused when replica lag passes 1 s
choices.feedback: Right: steady, resumable progress that never lets replicas fall behind what users notice.

choices.label: A single UPDATE statement run in a quiet hour
choices.feedback: One 80M-row transaction causes heavy lag even when quiet, and a late failure rolls back everything.

choices.label: Many parallel workers at full speed, to finish quickly
choices.feedback: Finishes sooner but floods the primary’s I/O, and replicas fall well behind the 2 s promise.

interactive.reveal: When the job may take a day, use the day. Throttling on replica lag keeps the user-visible promise, checkpoints make restarts cheap, and key-ordered chunks keep every chunk equally fast.

A backfill is the middle step of an expand-and-contract schema change
Throttling a batch job is backpressure applied to your own work
Long backfills usually run as background jobs with retries and progress
Deleting a large object’s children is a batch job like any other

title: Audit Trails in Code: Actors, Impersonation and Activity Logs
objectives: Carry the real actor, and the account they act for, from the request into every audit record, including jobs and service calls
Design support impersonation so every action is attributable, time-limited and tied to a reason
Record audits in shared code, including denials, and serve customer activity logs from the same records

cards.title: An actor context, set once per request
cards.body: Handlers should not build audit records from scratch. The middleware that authenticates a request creates an actor context: the actor’s id and type (user, staff, service or API key), the account acted on behalf of, the tenant, the request id and the source address. The audit helper reads that context, so every record has the same shape and nobody forgets the actor. Background jobs and calls to other services carry the context forward, in the job payload or in a token the receiver can verify.

cards.title: Worked example: who refunded order 81?
cards.body: A support agent clicks Refund; the API queues a job; the worker calls the payments service with its own credentials. If each hop records only its immediate caller, the payments service’s record says refund-worker refunded order 81, and the agent’s name stops at the API. Put the original actor (agent 17, acting for customer 5523, ticket SUP-4410) in the job payload and pass it on the service call, and have every hop record both: “caller refund-worker, initiated by agent 17 for customer 5523, ticket SUP-4410”.

cards.title: Support impersonation with an audit trail
cards.body: Acting as a customer is a separate, short-lived kind of session, never a shared login.
steps: The agent asks to act as a customer and gives a ticket number
The system checks the agent’s role and, for sensitive scopes, asks a second person to approve
It issues a short-lived session marked actor = agent, subject = customer
Every action in that session is recorded with both ids and the ticket
The session expires, and the customer’s activity log shows that support accessed the account

cards.title: Activity logs customers can see
cards.body: Many products show users and their admins a trail of their own: “New sign-in from Chrome on Windows, Pune”, “Asha changed the billing email”. Build these from the same audit records, filtered by tenant and permission, with action names turned into readable sentences and staff shown by role, such as “Support”, where policy says so. Enterprise customers often want an export or an API to feed their own security tools; scope it to their tenant and page it by time and id, not by offset.

cards.title: Trap: one audit call per handler, written by hand
cards.body: When every handler calls audit() itself after its work succeeds, some forget, and denied attempts are never recorded at all, because the handler returns its 403 before reaching the call. Put auditing in shared code: the authorisation layer records allow and deny decisions for sensitive actions, and the data-access layer records changes in the same transaction as the write. Thirty refused refund attempts from one account in a minute is exactly what an investigator wants to find.

questions.prompt: Refunds are issued by a queued job, and every refund in the audit trail shows the actor “refund-worker”. What fixes this?

choices.label: Run the worker under each agent’s own database login
Carry the original actor in the job payload and record it
Log the agent’s id to the debug log when queuing
Find the agent later by matching up timestamps

questions.explanation: a: database logins per person do not scale and still lose who acted for whom. b: correct, the job knows who asked for it, and every record can name both the agent and the worker. c: debug logs are sampled, rotated and not joined to the audit record. d: matching by time is guesswork the moment two agents act in the same second.

questions.prompt: A support agent signs in as a customer to debug an issue and changes the customer’s address. Who should the record show as the actor?

choices.label: The customer, as it was their session
The agent, acting on behalf of the customer
The support tool’s service account
Nobody, as it was only debugging

questions.explanation: a: the customer did not make the change, and a dispute would blame the wrong person. b: correct, record the real actor and the account they acted for. c: a shared service account hides which person acted. d: changes made while debugging are still changes to a customer’s data.

questions.prompt: Which setup best fits support staff who sometimes need to see a customer’s account?

choices.label: A shared support login that can open any account
A short session tied to a ticket, naming both people
The customer’s password, sent to support over chat
Permanent admin rights for every support agent

questions.explanation: a: a shared login cannot say which agent acted, and its access never ends. b: correct, the session expires, has a stated reason, and every action in it records the agent and the customer. c: it teaches customers to share passwords and makes the agent indistinguishable from the customer. d: standing admin rights give every agent far more access than any one ticket needs.

questions.prompt: Refund handlers call audit() after a refund succeeds. Which events will the trail miss?

choices.label: Refund attempts the policy check denied
Refunds above a set amount, such as ₹10,000
Refunds issued by admins rather than agents
Refunds that took longer than a second

questions.explanation: a: correct, a denied request returns before the audit call, so probing and abuse leave no trace; recording decisions in the authorisation layer fixes it. b: large refunds succeed like any other and are recorded. c: the handler runs the same way whoever the actor is. d: slow requests still reach the audit call when they succeed.

questions.prompt: An enterprise customer wants to pull its own audit records into its security tools every day. What fits best?

choices.label: A CSV that support emails to them on request
An API scoped to their tenant, paged by time and id
Read access to the shared audit table
A daily copy of the application’s debug logs

questions.explanation: a: manual exports are slow, irregular and easy to send to the wrong person. b: correct, tenant scoping keeps other customers’ records out, and keyset paging stays fast however far back the export reaches. c: the shared table holds every tenant’s records. d: debug logs are incomplete, unstructured for this purpose, and may contain other tenants’ data.

questions.prompt: Order how a support agent gets to act as a customer.

items.label: Each action in it is recorded with both ids and the ticket
The agent requests access and gives a ticket number
The session expires and appears in the customer’s activity log
A short-lived session is issued with actor and subject set
The system checks the agent’s role and any approval needed

questions.explanation: A reason comes first, authorisation before any access, and the session itself carries both identities, so every record written during it names the real actor.

questions.prompt: A tenant exports 30 million audit records through an API that returns 1,000 records per page, each page taking 0.2 s with keyset paging. How many minutes does the full export take?
assumptions: Pages are fetched one after another
Each page takes the same time
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with offset paging each page would skip all earlier rows and grow slower, so the same export would take many times longer; keyset paging keeps every page at 0.2 s.

flashcards.back: Set once by authentication: actor, on-behalf-of, tenant, request id; carried into jobs and service calls.
A short-lived, ticket-linked session that records both the agent and the customer.

flashcards.front: Where should denied attempts be recorded?
flashcards.back: In the authorisation layer, so a 403 is audited without each handler remembering.

mechanism.title: How a service attributes every action to someone
steps: The actor context is created where authentication happens. It names the actor and its type (a person, a staff member, a service, an API key), the account acted on behalf of, the tenant, the request id and the source address. Code reads it from request-scoped context; nothing below the middleware asks the caller who they are.

The context travels. Within a process it is request-scoped; across a queue it goes in the job payload; across services it goes in a token or header the receiver can verify. OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, for example, defines an act claim for “this service is acting for that user”. Each record keeps both the immediate caller and the originating actor.

Audits are written by shared code with stable action names such as refund.issue or role.grant. The authorisation layer records allow and deny decisions for sensitive actions; the data-access layer records changes in the same transaction as the write, so neither exists without the other. Handlers add only what is specific to them, such as the amount or the reason.

Impersonation and emergency access are their own kind of session: requested with a reason or ticket, approved by someone else for sensitive scopes, limited to minutes, visibly marked in the interface, recorded with both identities, and reviewed afterwards. Many products also tell the customer, through their activity log or a notification.

The same records serve readers. Customer-facing activity logs and exports are filtered by tenant and permission, translate action names into sentences, and page by time and id. Retention can differ by plan, and personal details stay out of the records, which refer to people by id, so a person’s data can be erased elsewhere while the trail stays intact.

useWhen: Admin panels, support tools, money movements and access to personal data.
Systems with background jobs or several services acting on a user’s behalf.
avoidWhen: Avoid recording only the immediate caller, such as a worker or service account.
Avoid shared support logins and hand-written audit calls in each handler.

rows: Who, for whom, and through what
Must be carried across every hop

numbers.title: Sizing a customer activity log
assumptions: About 5,000 audit records per tenant per month
About 600 bytes per record, indexes included
steps: Per month: 20,000 × 5,000 = 100M records.
In bytes: 100M × 600 bytes = 60 GB a month.
90-day retention holds about 180 GB; 1-year retention about 720 GB.
Keeping the last 90 days in fast storage and older months in cheaper storage keeps search quick for most readers.
numbers.result: An activity log is a product feature with a storage bill. Set retention per plan and keep recent months fast to search.

india.title: Support access at a lending company
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: support staff at a lending app sometimes need to see a borrower’s screens. They open a ticket-linked session that lasts 30 minutes; anything sensitive, such as changing bank details, needs a second agent’s approval. Every action records the agent, the borrower and the ticket, and fee waivers queued from the session carry the same context into the billing worker. The borrower’s activity page shows “Support viewed your account (ticket SUP-4410)”, and a monthly review searches the trail for agents with unusual numbers of waivers.

pitfalls.trap: “The worker made the change, so the actor is the worker.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d record the worker as the caller and the agent who asked as the actor, carried in the job payload.”

pitfalls.trap: “Support can just log in as the customer.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d use a short, ticket-linked impersonation session that records both the agent and the customer.”

takeaways: Build an actor context once per request and pass it into jobs and service calls.
Record both the originating actor and the immediate caller.
Make impersonation short-lived, reasoned and visible in the record.
Audit in shared code, including denials, and serve activity logs from the same records.

interactive.title: A refund through a queue
interactive.prompt: An agent clicks Refund. The API queues a job, and the worker calls the payments service with its own service credentials. Each component writes an audit record naming whoever called it. Months later a customer disputes the refund. What does the payments service’s record say?

choices.label: The refund was made by refund-worker
choices.feedback: Right: each hop saw only its immediate caller, so the agent’s name stopped at the API.

choices.label: The refund was made by the support agent
choices.feedback: Only if the agent’s identity travelled with the job; here the worker used only its own credentials.

choices.label: The refund was made by the customer
choices.feedback: The customer did not act, and nothing in the chain names them as the actor.

interactive.reveal: Carry the originating actor, the account acted for and the ticket through the job payload and service calls, and record them next to the immediate caller at every hop.

seeAlso.why: Authorisation decisions, including denials, are what audit records describe
Request ids tie audit records to the logs and traces of the same request
Activity-log exports page by time and id, not by offset
Making audit records tamper-evident and turning security events into detections

title: Holding Many Live Connections on the Server
objectives: Estimate the memory and file descriptors that many long-lived connections need
Deliver a message to a user connected to another server through pub/sub
Survive deploys and outages without a reconnect storm or lost messages

cards.title: A connection is a resource you hold
cards.body: Each open WebSocket or server-sent events stream holds a file descriptor, kernel socket buffers and some application state for as long as the user stays connected. At an estimated 20 KB per connection, 100,000 connections need about 2 GB on one server. Raise the per-process file-descriptor limit (a soft limit of 1,024 is a common default), and use event-driven I/O so one thread serves many sockets instead of a thread per connection.

cards.title: Reaching a user on another server
cards.body: Gateways hold the sockets; a pub/sub layer connects them.
steps: User A is connected to gateway 3, user B to gateway 7
A’s message reaches the chat service through gateway 3
The service publishes it to B’s channel in a pub/sub system
Gateway 7, subscribed to B’s channel, writes it down B’s connection
If B is offline, it waits in storage until B reconnects and asks for it

cards.title: Worked example: a reconnect storm
cards.body: A gateway holding 200,000 connections restarts. If every client reconnects within about a second, the fleet faces 200,000 TLS handshakes and authentications at once. Against an estimated capacity of 10,000 a second, that is a 20 s backlog; clients time out and retry, adding still more. If clients instead wait a random delay spread over 60 s before reconnecting, the load is about 3,300 a second, well within capacity.

cards.title: Heartbeats and graceful drains
cards.body: Load balancers and home routers silently drop connections that look idle, and the server gets no close event. Send a ping every 30 s or so and close the connection if two in a row go unanswered. For deploys, drain instead of killing: take the gateway out of the load balancer, send connected clients a reconnect message that tells each to wait a random delay, give them a few minutes to move, then close what remains and stop.

cards.title: Trap: treating the socket as the delivery guarantee
cards.body: A message written to a socket can still be lost if the connection dies before the client reads it. Give each message a per-conversation sequence number and store it before sending. The client remembers the last number it processed and, on reconnecting, asks for everything after it; the server replays from storage. Live delivery is the fast path, and the replay on reconnect is what makes delivery reliable.

questions.prompt: A gateway holds 250,000 connections at about 16 KB each. Roughly how much memory do the connections use?

choices.label: About 400 MB
About 4 GB
About 16 GB
About 40 GB

questions.explanation: a: that is ten times too small. b: correct, 250,000 × 16 KB = 4,000,000 KB, about 4 GB. c: that would be 64 KB each. d: ten times too large.

questions.prompt: User B is connected to a different server from user A. How does A’s message reach B?

choices.label: A’s server opens a socket to B’s device
B’s client polls A’s server every second
B’s server receives it through pub/sub
The load balancer copies it to every server

questions.explanation: a: devices accept no inbound connections; they connect out to gateways. b: B does not know which server A uses, and polling every second defeats the open connection. c: correct, B’s gateway subscribes to B’s channel and pushes what is published there. d: load balancers route requests; they do not broadcast messages to servers.

questions.prompt: After a gateway restart, every dropped client reconnects at once and the replacement gateway falls over. What prevents this?

choices.label: Longer heartbeat intervals on the server
Reconnecting at once to another gateway
A higher file-descriptor limit
A random, growing delay before reconnects

questions.explanation: a: heartbeats detect dead connections; they do not spread out reconnects. b: moving the whole crowd to another gateway moves the overload with it. c: the bottleneck is handshakes per second, not open descriptors. d: correct, jittered backoff spreads the reconnects over time so the fleet absorbs them.

questions.prompt: Idle connections die after a few minutes with no close event on the server. What is the usual fix?

choices.label: Raise the server’s read timeout to an hour
Have every client reconnect each minute
Ping every 30 s; close if pongs stop
Switch from server-sent events to polling

questions.explanation: a: the middlebox drops the idle connection regardless of the server’s timeout. b: constant reconnects add handshake load for no reason. c: correct, regular pings keep the path active and reveal dead connections so the server can free them. d: polling avoids idle sockets but gives up the push model and adds request load.

questions.prompt: A phone loses signal for 20 s during a chat. How does it get the messages it missed?

choices.label: It reconnects and asks for all after its last id
The server resends everything since login
The socket holds them until signal returns
It does not; chats show only live messages

questions.explanation: a: correct, sequence numbers let the client ask for exactly the gap, which the server replays from storage. b: resending everything wastes bandwidth and duplicates what was already shown. c: the old connection is dead; its buffers are gone. d: users expect to see what was sent while they were away.

questions.prompt: Order a graceful deploy of one connection gateway.

items.label: Close the connections that remain
Send connected clients a reconnect hint with a random delay
Stop the process and start the new version
Stop sending it new connections at the load balancer
Wait a few minutes while clients move

questions.explanation: Draining moves clients over minutes, at a pace the other gateways can absorb, instead of dropping them all at once.

questions.prompt: 200,000 dropped clients reconnect with jitter, spread evenly over 50 s. About how many handshakes per second must the fleet absorb?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with no jitter all 200,000 arrive within about a second, fifty times this rate.

flashcards.back: A file descriptor, socket buffers and app state, held for as long as it is open.

flashcards.front: Reaching a user on another gateway?
flashcards.back: Publish to the user’s channel; the gateway holding their socket subscribes and pushes.
Jittered, growing reconnect delays, and draining gateways gradually on deploy.

mechanism.title: How a gateway fleet holds connections and delivers messages
steps: Clients open a long-lived connection to a gateway: a WebSocket for two-way traffic or a server-sent events stream for server-to-client updates. The gateway authenticates the connection once, records which user it belongs to, and keeps it open. Gateways do little else, so they can be scaled and restarted separately from the services that hold the business logic.

Each gateway serves many sockets from a few threads with event-driven I/O, such as epoll on Linux, which tells the process which sockets are ready instead of parking a thread on each. Its capacity is set by memory per connection, the file-descriptor limit, CPU for heartbeats and messages, and above all how many new handshakes it can complete per second.

When a service wants to reach a user, it does not need to know which gateway holds them. It publishes to the user’s channel in a pub/sub system, and the gateway holding that user subscribes to the channel while the connection is open. Messages are also written to storage with a sequence number before publishing, so a client that was away can catch up.

Connections fail all the time: phones change networks, routers drop idle flows, gateways restart. Heartbeats find dead connections so their resources are freed. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and random jitter, and on reconnecting they send the last sequence number they processed, so the server replays only the gap. Delivery is at least once, so clients ignore duplicates by sequence number.

Deploys and incidents are where fleets break. A gateway being replaced is drained: removed from the load balancer, its clients told to reconnect after a random delay, then closed after a few minutes. Capacity is planned for the reconnect rate after losing a whole gateway, not only for the steady number of connections, and admission control sheds handshakes beyond what the fleet can complete.

useWhen: Chat, live scores, notifications, collaborative editing and dashboards that push updates.
Any feature where users stay connected for minutes or hours.
avoidWhen: Avoid a thread per connection; memory and scheduling fall over long before sockets do.
Avoid relying on the open socket alone for delivery; store and replay by sequence number.

rows: Channels per user or room, sharded pub/sub

numbers.title: Sizing a gateway
assumptions: A 32 GB gateway, keeping half its RAM free for headroom
About 5,000 new handshakes per second per gateway (an estimate)
steps: Memory: 16 GB ÷ 16 KB ≈ 1,000,000 connections.
If that gateway dies, its clients must reconnect elsewhere. Spread over 60 s, that is about 16,700 handshakes per second.
At about 5,000 handshakes per second per gateway, absorbing it takes about 3.3 gateways’ worth of spare handshake capacity.
So a fleet often holds far fewer connections per gateway than memory allows, such as 200,000, to keep failures absorbable.
numbers.result: Memory says how many connections a gateway can hold; the reconnect rate after a failure says how many it should hold.

india.title: Live scores during a big match
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: a sports app pushes ball-by-ball updates to millions of fans during a cricket final. Each fan’s app holds a connection to a gateway subscribed to the match channel. When a wicket falls, many more users open the app at once, so the team pre-scales gateways before the match, uses jittered reconnects, and drains gateways slowly if one must be replaced mid-match. Updates carry sequence numbers, so an app that dropped off in a tunnel fetches exactly the balls it missed.

pitfalls.trap: “WebSockets scale to millions; we will just open them.”
pitfalls.say: “Each one costs memory and a descriptor, and a failed gateway causes a reconnect storm, so I’d size for that.”

pitfalls.trap: “If we wrote it to the socket, the user got it.”
pitfalls.say: “The connection can die first, so I’d store messages with sequence numbers and replay the gap on reconnect.”

takeaways: Each live connection holds memory and a file descriptor.
Pub/sub lets any service reach a user on any gateway.
Jittered reconnects and gradual drains prevent reconnect storms.
Sequence numbers and replay on reconnect make delivery reliable.

interactive.title: Ten gateways, no pub/sub
interactive.prompt: A chat service runs 10 gateways and users are assigned to them at random. Each gateway delivers a message only if the recipient is connected to that same gateway. What do users see?

choices.label: Only about 1 message in 10 arrives live
choices.feedback: Right: sender and recipient share a gateway only about a tenth of the time.

choices.label: Every message arrives, a little more slowly
choices.feedback: Nothing carries messages between gateways, so most never reach the recipient’s socket.

choices.label: Every message arrives twice
choices.feedback: Duplicates come from retries, not from missing cross-gateway delivery.

interactive.reveal: Connections are spread over many servers, so delivery needs a layer that finds the right one: pub/sub channels per user or room, or a lookup of which gateway holds each user. Store messages too, so the ones that miss live delivery are fetched on reconnect.

Admission control and load shedding protect gateways during reconnect storms
Keep-alive and idle timeouts at each hop decide when a held connection is cut
Every live connection holds a file descriptor, so the open-files limit caps a gateway
